LD 235 Resolve, Regarding the Operation and Future Capacity of State-owned Landfills
Testimony NEITHER IN SUPPORT OR OPPOSITION Joint Committee on Environment and Natural Resources
Public Hearing Submitted by  Jacquelyn Elliott
March 17, 2025
Chair Senator Tepler; Chair Representative Doudera; and Honorable Committee Members:
Thank you for the opportunity to offer testimony on LD 235 NEITER IN SUPPORT OR OPPOSITION. My name is Jackie Elliott and I live in Waterboro. For decades I have been an environmental health and justice advocate working for waste management policy that prioritizes conservation of resources and incorporates life-cycle implications; reduces the amount and toxicity of waste generated; maximizes safe disposal capacity and safeguards public and environmental health; and centers the rights of communities most impacted with permit decisions for facilities.
LD 235 would require the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) to evaluate the potential, costs, and benefits if the State were to acquire ownership of the former paper mill landfill in the Town of Jay to provide disposal capacity for wastewater treatment facility biosolids and other special wastes. The biosolids waste1 stream is ostensibly driving Maine's landfill capacity needs and is an underlying argument for expansion of the State-owned Juniper Ridge Landfill in Old Town. The matter of biosolids management and the accompanying issue of contamination with `forever' per -and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) is integral to any discussion. It is evident that current waste management disposal methods are not sustainable and PFAS treatment methods2 do not yet adequately address the emerging needs.
The State did the right thing when they banned spreading biosolids on farmland for use as fertilizer. We are working through the painful results of that mis-guided policy - polluted soil and water, contaminated livestock, wildlife, and crops; human bodies burdened with high blood serum levels of PFAS. The moratorium on land-spreading biosolids continues to be a targeted excuse for why we are under stress with disposal. The pressure mounts to find more appropriate ways to manage biosolids and address the PFAS contamination of landfill leachate

and wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) biosolids to meet the standards of increasing effluent regulation. Emerging research is indicating there is no safe level for PFAS exposure3.
State ownership of a landfill for the purpose of managing dried biosolids and PFAScontaminated media would have benefits if it were properly regulated and operated. If the State were to exercise it options4 as a market participant, a landfill could be maximized for the public benefit of Maine citizens and the State's needs for disposal capacity. To be successful, the model would have to avoid the pitfalls of the history and current operations of Juniper Ridge and provide a mechanism for maintenance and monitoring in perpetuity.
PFAS contamination will continue to push materials management policy until we turn off the tap on the front end of the unnecessary production and use of PFAS. Landfills will be the most likely disposal option for the foreseeable future. Construction of a double-lined, drytomb landfill5 secured as a hazardous waste landfill could be utilized for dried WWTP and landfill leachate biosolids that have been treated for PFAS removal. Such a landfill could also provide safer disposal for contaminated media from PFAS removal operations.
Biosolids and PFAS-contaminated media should not be landfilled with raw municipal solid waste (MSW) or other wet wastes. Juniper Ridge is an inappropriate disposal option and increases threats to public health and the environment. Presently, the citizens of Old Town and other neighbors of Juniper Ridge are assuming the greatest risks associated with biosolids disposal. The rights to a healthy environment for these citizens including members of the Penobscot Indian Nation are not respected as they, and much of Penobscot County, function as a `sacrifice zone' for poor materials management policy and regulation. This is an untenable situation.
LD 235 asks the Department of Administrative and Financial Services (DAFS), Bureau of General Services (BGS) and DEP to evaluate options for amending the operating services agreement (OSA), between the State and Casella Waste Systems, the operator of Juniper Ridge. For years citizens have been expressing concerns with landfill operations and the lack of transparency and oversight. A report on these matters with recommendations and legislation to address them would be welcomed by Maine citizens.
The DEP has already approved the Public Benefit Determination (PBD) for the proposed expansion of Juniper Ridge. The approval is currently under appeal. The request for

DAFS and BGS to initiate a process to amend the OSA prior to any PBD approval is a moot point. However, the specific provisions cited are familiar ground that has occupied past efforts before this Committee and the Legislature. There are current citizen-initiated endeavors seeking similar outcomes. LD 235 wants:
- Casella to disclose to BGS the terms and conditions of all contracts and agreements with its contractors, subcontractors and customers about the use, operation. and maintenance of the landfill. The public wants that information to be available to them, where possible, for the sake of transparency. The public additionally argues that identifying the sources, types, and amounts of waste landfilled would provide a more accurate account of how Juniper Ridge is being utilized for disposal capacity of Mainegenerated waste. A clear definition for Maine-generated waste that does not involve semantics, would be progress.
- LD 235 requires Casella to implement and operate technology, to treat leachate to remove PFAS. Citizens want regulation to meet drinking water standards6 before treated leachate effluent can be discharged to surface waters.
- Minimally, there should be resolution for the concerns raised with LD 235 before Casella/BGS can file an application with DEP for a permit to expand Juniper Ridge. The issues raised with this Resolve deserve thoughtful consideration by the
Committee and it is hoped that LD 235 will be a catalyst to develop effective and just responses that provide particular benefit for Old Town and its residents as the site of the Juniper Ridge Landfill as well as represent value for all Maine citizens. Materials management policy that focuses on the front end should be the beginning: RETHINK. REDUCE. REUSE. REPURPOSE. REFILL. REPAIR. RECYCLE. COMPOST.
Thank you for considering my comments.

10037637:
Testimony Neither for Nor Against LD 235, Resolve, Regarding the Operation and Future Capacity of State-Owned Landfills
Vanessa Berry, NRCM Sustainable Maine Program Manager March 17, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Environment and Natural Resources, my name is Vanessa Berry, and I serve as the Sustainable Maine Program Manager for the Natural Resources Council of Maine (NRCM). I appreciate the opportunity to testify Neither For Nor Against LD 235.
This bill directs the Department of Environmental Protection to evaluate two potential opportunities in Maine's materials management system: assessing the viability of an existing landfill in Jay and reviewing the Operating Services Agreement for Juniper Ridge Landfill (JRL) in Old Town.
NRCM strongly supports Maine's waste reduction and diversion goals. We work closely with residents, municipalities, businesses, schools, and organizations to promote waste reduction at the source, transition away from single-use materials, and encourage recycling and composting whenever possible. While our top priority is to promote the minimization of waste, we recognize that landfill disposal will remain a necessary part of our system. As such, we strongly believe that landfills must be well regulated to ensure that they are safe for public health and the environment, and they must be responsibly managed with long-term community health and safety in mind.
We have significant concerns about Maine's current waste disposal practices, particularly regarding transparency and management at JRL. Community members have long reported air, land, and water quality issues associated with JRL's operation. Expanding landfills indefinitely is not a sustainable solution, yet we acknowledge the need for appropriate waste disposal options.
For this reason, we support the Committee's efforts to reassess Maine's agreement for operating JRL and to explore alternative disposal options. However, we urge careful reflection on lessons learned in Old Town to avoid replicating existing landfill challenges in Jay. While the former Jay paper mill site may offer a short-term solution, it will be critically important to fully consider potential long-term environmental and community impacts before establishing a new State-owned landfill with a contracted operator.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
10037177:
Comments Neither for nor AgainstL.D. 235; Resolve, Regarding the Operation and Future Capacity of State-owned Landfills
Written testimony provided by Victor Horton, Executive Director of MRRA
The Maine Resource Recovery Association ("MRRA") isa nonprofit organization committed to supporting professional and sustainable materials management in Maine. Established in 1984, MRRA serves over 160 municipalities through its work to provide ongoing education on waste regulations, evolving waste streams, and best practices. We also assist in operating 60 transfer stations and recycling centers and help members find markets for recyclable materials, reinforcing Maine's commitment to resource recovery.
We have carefully reviewed L.D. 235 and have taken a neither for nor against position on the bill overall. However, we do offer the following comments regarding one specific section of the bill.
Section 1. Report on Jay landfill
The fundamental purpose of Maine's collective solid waste management system ("System") is to provide safe and adequate disposal capacity for the wastes generated by society. If that fundamental purpose is not met, the environmental impacts would be significant; and any efforts to implement programs that move waste management "up the hierarchy" become of secondary priority. To-date, the State has essentially been reliant on capacity at a single facility, namely Juniper Ridge Landfill ("JRL") to provide this capacity, and ultimately the State has little control over how that capacity is utilized.
The opportunity presented by the potentially-available disposal capacity at the defunct paper mill in Jay should be fully-vetted to determine its' potential value to the State for this fundamental purpose; and to preserve the gains made in our materials management strategy.
More specifically, we believe the Department of Administrative and Financial Services, Bureau of General Services ("the Bureau") should be the lead agency for this effort, with the Department of Environmental Protection providing input limited to the environmental suitability of the site and the landfill

design. The Bureau's evaluation should be from a more comprehensive perspective of needed capacity relative to generation sources, waste types, transportation planning, host community impacts, how the capacity could be utilized in conjunction with other disposal facilities, etc.
In other words - the overall value of the capacity to the State, municipalities, and businesses. As noted in the bill, this evaluation should not be limited to disposal of only "wastewater treatment plant sludge and special wastes," but should also consider the current and potential future need for disposal of other waste types such as municipal solid waste and demolition debris.
The MRRA and its members stand ready to provide any additional input during this process; and/or with regard to the eventual findings and conclusions of the report.
On behalf of our members, we thank you for the opportunity to provide input on this bill.
Victor Horton
